newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Koreans fret over industrial chaos.
newsitem.headline: South Koreans fret over industrial chaos.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party has garnered as many brick bats as plaudits by ramming through a controversial labour law.
While some Koreans on Friday criticised the shock move, which has sparked nationwide strikes, as an act of political vandalism, others said it demonstrated resolve.

There was anxiety about what it would all mean for the daily lives of citizens battling through a strike-hit subway system, or searching for medical attention at hospitals where nurses have abandoned their wards.
Opinions varied on who is right, and who is wrong.
"I feel robbed," said car salesman Kang Sung-ro, who compared the tactics of the ruling New Korea Party to those adopted by previous military-backed governments.
"It was like taking a time machine and going backwards," he said. "I can't believe they passed a law like that."
Yang Gum-yong, a middle-aged taxi driver, was more even-handed. "I think both the government and the workers are wrong," he said.
"I used to be a union member, and even if union pluralism is permitted workers will only fight more among themselves. They don't know how to work as one."
He was referring to a provision of the new labour law allowing more than one union in each work place.
Yet Yang, too, was irked by the government's sly manoevering -- for which it has publicly apologised.
"If the new law is so great, why did the government have to pass it so secretly. I think the ruling party will try to use this period of confusion to help them in next year's elections," he said.
Presidential polls are scheduled for next December, and although President Kim Young-sam cannot seek a second term he needs public backing to anoint a successor.

Some Seoul residents, however, sympathised with the government's dilemma: it holds a majority in parliament yet was unable to pass the labour law because opposition deputies physically blocked the vote.
In the end, the bill was adopted literally under cover of darkness -- in a hastily-convened dawn session on Thursday of the National Assembly while many opposition deputies were sleeping.

"The government had to do something to pass the law. The government needs to find security for the country," said Choi Won-suk, a student from Pusan, Korea's second largest city. "The opposition went too far in blocking the National Assembly."
"I feel really sad," said Choi Dae-shin, 74, a farmer from Cholla province, an opposition stronghold.
"We elected members of parliament to represent us, and they only represent their own political interests. What they did was unethical and inhumane."
Kim Soon-ik, 38, whose husband is also a worker but not part of a union, was understanding.
"It will be difficult if subway workers strike, but we must understand that the government won't take notice of them otherwise," she said.
Car salesman Kang fretted about his livelihood if the industrial action dragged on.
"I feel suffocated," he said. "I'm busy organising my orders. If the strike goes on for a long time I won't have any cars to sell."
